coachingPoints: Never use film to embarrass a player publicly; correct sensitive mistakes privately.
Individual film — five minutes one-on-one — is often more powerful than team film.
Let players clip their own games; ownership deepens learning.
Track whether film corrections actually show up in the next game.
commonMistakes: Showing too many clips in a single session and losing attention.
Only showing mistakes and never the good plays worth repeating.
Lecturing through the entire session without asking players what they see.
Watching film without connecting it to reps in the next practice.
description: How coaches should use film — what to clip, how to present it, and turning video sessions into real improvement.
gameSituations: Post-game review: three things we did well, two things to fix.
Preparing for an opponent: showing their favorite actions before practice.
Individual development: reviewing a guard's pick-and-roll reads from last weekend.

howTo.detail: Each session has one focus — transition defense, spacing, closeouts — and you only show clips that serve it. A theme turns random clips into a lesson.
howTo.title: Clip with a theme

howTo.detail: Fifteen to twenty minutes maximum. Attention dies after that, especially with youth players. A short session players remember beats a long one they tune out.
howTo.title: Keep it short

howTo.detail: Lead with two or three positive clips before corrections. Players learn from models of what to do, not just examples of what went wrong.
howTo.title: Show good and bad

howTo.detail: Pause the clip and ask "what do you see?" before explaining. Players who discover the answer retain it; players who are told it forget it.
howTo.title: Ask, don't tell

howTo.detail: Every session ends with one or two specific things to fix in the next practice. Film without follow-up action is just entertainment.
howTo.title: End with action

howTo.detail: Schedule film weekly. Sporadic film feels like punishment; routine film feels like development. Consistency builds a film culture.
howTo.title: Make film a habit

title: Film Study for Coaches
whatIsIt: Film study is the coach's most powerful teaching tool: real game footage that shows players exactly what happened, not what they remember happening. Used well, it accelerates learning in ways practice alone cannot — players see their spacing, their rotations, their decisions.
Effective film sessions are short, focused, and interactive. Ten great clips with discussion beat forty clips of lecture. The goal is not to show everything — it is to change one or two behaviors.
whyItMatters: Players cannot fix what they cannot see. Film closes the gap between perception and reality — the player who thought they sprinted back sees themselves jogging. Teams that watch film regularly develop faster basketball IQ and stop repeating the same mistakes.
Film also makes coaching conversations objective. "Watch this clip" ends arguments that "you need to play harder" starts. The camera does not have favorites.
